```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(descriptr)
library(dplyr)
```

## Introduction

This document introduces you to a basic set of functions that describe data
continuous data. The other two vignettes introduce you to functions that
describe categorical data and visualization options.

## Data

The `wholesale_customers` data set contains annual spending by 440 wholesale
customers on six product categories. It has eight columns: the two factors
`channel` and `region`, and six integer columns with the annual spend on fresh
products, milk, groceries, frozen products, detergents and paper, and
delicatessen products. The source does not specify a currency.

```{r egdata}
str(wholesale_customers)
```

## Data Screening

The `ds_screener()` function will screen a data set and return the following:
- Column/Variable Names
- Data Type
- Levels (in case of categorical data)
- Number of missing observations
- % of missing observations

The data set is complete: none of the eight variables has a missing value.

```{r screener}
ds_screener(wholesale_customers)
```

## Summary Statistics

The `ds_summary_stats` function returns a comprehensive set of statistics 
including measures of location, variation, symmetry and extreme observations.
Annual spending on fresh products averages 12000.30, with a median of 8504 and
a standard deviation of 12647.33. The distribution is right-skewed (skewness
2.56).

```{r summary}
ds_summary_stats(wholesale_customers, fresh)
```

You can pass multiple variables as shown below. Milk spending averages 5796.27
with a median of 3627, and is even more right-skewed (skewness 4.05).

```{r summary2}
ds_summary_stats(wholesale_customers, fresh, milk)
```

If you do not specify any variables, it will detect all the continuous 
variables in the data set and return summary statistics for each of them.

## Frequency Distribution

The `ds_freq_table` function creates frequency tables for continuous variables. 
The default number of intervals is 5. With four intervals, 400 of the 440
customers (90.91%) spend less than 28040 on fresh products, and only one
customer (0.23%) falls in the top interval of 84114 to 112151.

```{r fcont}
ds_freq_table(wholesale_customers, fresh, 4)
```

### Histogram

A `plot()` method has been defined which will generate a histogram.

```{r fcont_hist, fig.width=7, fig.height=7, fig.align='centre'}
k <- ds_freq_table(wholesale_customers, fresh, 4)
plot(k)
```

## Auto Summary

If you want to view summary statistics and frequency tables of all or subset of
variables in a data set, use `ds_auto_summary_stats()`.

```{r auto-summary}
ds_auto_summary_stats(wholesale_customers, fresh, milk)
```

## Group Summary

The `ds_group_summary()` function returns descriptive statistics of a continuous
variable for the different levels of a categorical variable. Hotel/restaurant/cafe
customers spend 13475.56 on fresh products on average, compared with 8904.32 for
retail customers; the medians are 9581.5 and 5993.5.

```{r gsummary}
k <- ds_group_summary(wholesale_customers, channel, fresh)
k
```

`ds_group_summary()` returns a tibble which can be used for further analysis.

```{r gsummary_tibble}
k$tidy_stats
```

### Box Plot

A `plot()` method has been defined for comparing distributions.

```{r gsum_boxplot, fig.width=7, fig.height=7, fig.align='centre'}
k <- ds_group_summary(wholesale_customers, channel, fresh)
plot(k)
```

### Multiple Variables

If you want grouped summary statistics for multiple variables in a data set, use
`ds_auto_group_summary()`. Grouping fresh spending by region, customers in the
other region spend 12533.47 on average, against 11101.73 in Lisbon and 9887.68
in Porto.

```{r auto-group-summary}
ds_auto_group_summary(wholesale_customers, channel, region, fresh)
```

### Combination of Categories

To look at the descriptive statistics of a continuous variable for different 
combinations of levels of two or more categorical variables, use 
`ds_group_summary_interact()`. Retail customers in Lisbon have the lowest mean
fresh spending (5200), while hotel/restaurant/cafe customers in the other region
have the highest (13878).

```{r interact-summary}
ds_group_summary_interact(wholesale_customers, fresh, channel, region)
```

## Multiple Variable Statistics 

The `ds_tidy_stats()` function returns summary/descriptive statistics for 
variables in a data frame/tibble. Fresh products have the highest mean annual
spending (12000), followed by groceries (7951) and milk (5796).

```{r multistats}
ds_tidy_stats(wholesale_customers, fresh, milk, grocery)
```

## Measures

If you want to view the measure of location, variation, symmetry, percentiles 
and extreme observations as tibbles, use the below functions. All of them, 
except for `ds_extreme_obs()` will work with single or multiple variables. If 
you do not specify the variables, they will return the results for all the 
continuous variables in the data set.

#### Measures of Location

```{r mloc}
ds_measures_location(wholesale_customers)
```

#### Measures of Variation

Delicatessen has the largest coefficient of variation (184.94) and fresh
products the smallest (105.39).

```{r mvar}
ds_measures_variation(wholesale_customers)
```

#### Measures of Symmetry

All six product categories are right-skewed, with skewness ranging from 2.56 for
fresh products to 11.15 for delicatessen.

```{r msym}
ds_measures_symmetry(wholesale_customers)
```

#### Percentiles

Half of the customers spend less than 8504 on fresh products, and the 99th
percentile is 56082.61.

```{r mperc}
ds_percentiles(wholesale_customers)
```

#### Extreme Observations

The largest fresh purchase is 112151 (observation 182); the smallest is 3
(observations 96 and 339).

```{r mextreme}
ds_extreme_obs(wholesale_customers, fresh)
```
